written.myAnswer: Almost all an atom’s mass is concentrated in its nucleus because the nucleus contains protons and neutrons, which are much more massive than electrons.
Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons (different atomic numbers), and therefore have different properties.
The second shell is farther from the positively charged nucleus than the first shell, so an electron in it has greater energy.
The gas pressure is lowered so its particles are farther apart. Electrons can then travel farther between collisions, gain enough energy, and produce cathode rays.

Classically, an electron was pictured as revolving around the nucleus in a definite orbit or shell with a fixed energy. In the modern view, its position is described in terms of probability; its exact location and path cannot be known with complete certainty.

Cathode rays produced with different gases and electrodes had the same properties and the same charge-to-mass ratio, showing that electrons are present in all elements. Positive rays led to the identification of the proton: the hydrogen nucleus, which Rutherford showed is present in the nuclei of other elements.
An ordinary hydrogen atom has a nucleus containing one proton and one electron outside the nucleus. Its most common form has no neutron.

In Bohr’s model, electrons were pictured as revolving around a central nucleus in shells, like planets around the Sun. The comparison is not exact: in the modern model electrons do not have precisely known paths, and their locations are described by probabilities.
